source_checks.quote: Abstract The main aim of the study was to replicate and extend van Prooijen's findings on how education and its outcomes (cognitive complexity, subjective social standing, self‐esteem, a feeling of control and powerlessness, cognitive reflection, epistemic curiosity and scientific reasoning) predict conspiracy beliefs. In two studies (Study 1: N = 497, Mage = 49.06, SDage = 14.92; Study 2: N = 482, Mage = 47.45, SDage = 15.87), subjective socioeconomic status and cognitive reflection (Study 1) and a feeling of powerlessness and scientific reasoning (Study 2) contributed to the negative relationship between education level and belief in conspiracy theories.

source_checks.quote: In the current study, we used eye tracking to investigate the effects of intranasal OT on emotional empathy and visual attention to different features of real life pictures in the MET. Results first confirmed previous findings that OT increases emotional empathy in both negative and positive emotional contexts ( Hurlemann et al., 2010 ; Geng et al., 2018a , b ).

source_checks.quote: Here we report a study building on our previous work. We retained our previous sample of 10 women with PMDD and 15 healthy comparison women (cohort 1) and added a second independent cohort of 24 women with PMDD and 61 healthy comparison women (cohort 2). All participants underwent the same ovarian steroid hormone manipulation paradigm. We evaluated differences between cohorts, attempted to replicate our original findings of a differential behavioral sensitivity to otherwise similar changes in ovarian steroids in women with PMDD compared to healthy comparison women (3), and examined several as yet unanswered questions about the effects of ovarian steroids on symptoms in these women.
